I got to thinking (mainly due to this recent thread by the ever questioning u/profanion), and I can't say I really have a good "rule" or standard for good controls in any given genre, and I can't really explain why some controls "feel clunky," or just don't work. I know if the character's response time to input is bad, the game is going to suffer, but lots of games have characters that respond just fine to input, and yet, their controls are awful. I know that awkward button mapping can make for bad controls, but most games have buttons mapped fine as well. I usually can't explain why, I just know when controls are good, or bad. So, what do you think? What are some of those defining defining of bad controls? And bonus, what's some defining characteristics of good controls?
In your opinion, what exactly makes bad controls bad?

We could call controls bad if the game and level design isn't based on those controls but expects you to complete the game like the controls were responsive.

For an example, controls in Super Meat Boy and Dustforce are super tight. This means that the game can demand the players to make very precise maneuvers. Controls in LocoRoco are loose as you control a physics-based blob indirectly. This is not usually a problem as the levels are forgiving. However, LocoRoco: Midnight Carnival decided to make hard levels and that's where the game suffered.
So the consideration also must be on design at the same time? Interesting way of thinking about it. Controls are the way you're navigating the environment, after all.

Remember the game Nut & Milk or Ice Climbers. Both of those games have level designs that don't take its jump physics into consideration (+ dodgy collision detection in Ice Climbers). This makes you feel like the game is not playing fair as you bounce into and from walls.

On the other hand, forgiving level and game design in Octodad are perfectly suited for the wonky controls and physics of the game.

Same would go to Volgarr the Viking. The level and enemy design is designed for you to take its limited air control during jump into consideration.

I'd say like this: if I'm unable to enact my intentions in the game effectively through its controls. Sometimes I die because of poor planning, poor execution, or just not reacting in time. But I never want to be in a situation where I know exactly what to do but I'm just unable to enact those intentions effectively and so I fail.

Basically this. If I do the correct actions but still fail purely because the game refused to follow up on my input accurately and on time then the controls are bad and it becomes frustrating to play the game.

Exactly! And there are some gray spots, like aiming in a FPS game: I might be playing with the wrong sensitivity, or using a different magnification scope than is right for me; neither of these things are the game's fault. But when a game has poor controls and I'm not able to make my character do what I'm intending him to do, it's immediately noticeable.
gotta be nautural: buttons mapped to use and flow with no awkward reaches, secondly pure responsuveness.

Lag between when you input commands and when game registers them, or if the character movements are awkward, and no amount of practice with controls can fix that.

Contrived controls are fine, so long as they work smoothly once you get the hang of them. Kid Icarus: Uprising practically takes three hands to play and gave lefties like me the middle finger, but within a few levels I'd gotten a good grasp on how to manage everything at once, and a control system for that game with less to manage sounds terrible to me, because it was so nice to have the amount of control you did.
Bad controls are mostly about responsiveness and accuracy, like you said, but it's very hard to measure this, because sometimes it's almost imperceptible.
Shitty, annoying camera angles. Frustrating context buttons.

Mass Effect 2: chase down the android assassin lady in this scripted sequence. Press sprint, it interprets as "cover" and you stick to the nearest wall while she runs away and you dodge invisible bullets. Infuriating! Cover/Sprint/Use all on one button, worst idea ever, and translated straight to PC! Scripted sequence where you couldn't win was the icing on the cake after multiple reloads. I'm pretty sure I got close enough in the end...

If i press a button, i want it to do something at that moment, not a second later. Also mouse drift, some games have terrible mouse acceleration that you cannot disable causing you to always miss a target.

If you can aim at something with muscle memory, then i consider that good controls. Especially important in games where you might want to speed run. It has to be predictive most of the time.

I think the main example of controls not working is when you see a lazy port from Console to PC. What usually ends up happening - and I'll use Watch Dogs as an example - is that the smoothing of movement that is generally needed for consoles due to the nature of their clunky controls becomes painfully aware on a PC. Console controllers (and games) sacrifice accuracy for interactivity which is good in that environment, but on a PC you want accuracy in your movement. You don't want the speed up/slow down effect when you're trying to aim. Compare the aiming motions in the first Max Payne - both games are third person shooters but since Max Payne was developed for PC you get the accurate movement of your aiming.

I guess what I'm saying is, controls not made for the platform it is played on is going to suffer. The same applies when porting PC to console.
When I have to make "the claw" to make any sort of action. Looking at you MGS 1, 2, and 3.
Bad controls= no option to customize every control key for your own comfort.

delayed reaction, floaty/slidey feeling, too abrubt in slowing down or speeding up(with no bridging speed), especially when jumping, losing all control and momentum, and not being able to change arch. sticking keys(especially in key combination controls or context sensitive controls), having things do counter productive things bound to same button or close to, having not enough intuitively useful functions by easy access of single buttons. and lastly, relying on gimmicks, like microphone controlling, movement controlling (gyroscope in controller or external camera or light bar sensor), things that take you out of your usual warmed up flow of key pressing.

Depends entirely on context. For example, in a first person shooter you want turning that is slow and smooth at minor inclines but a rapid snap when you push your stick all the way. Platformers need a jump that triggers instantly. Melee combat games need to instantly stop an attack if you hit defend/dodge.

Those are the ones that come to me off the top of my head

Bad controls are bad if I can't rebind them the way I want them (keypad + mouse).

They are bad if the controls are situational and; the situational effects are unrelated or the controls have so many situational effects that it's hard to keep track.

Camera-jacking. When the game forces your camera to look at a specific thing (commonly boss monsters) or in a specific direction (Tomb Raider 2013 when LC is running through collapsing ruins).

Anything involving QTEs. (not sure if relevant to this thread)

Low frame rates. 30fps is much less responsive than 60fps.

Sometimes, games will animate badly, too. If MegaMan had 0.5s of animation before he jumped, then no matter how responsive the controls are they're not going to seem responsive.

There's also just poor design. Maybe the character should move/jump a little quicker, or a little farther. If Rock up there only jumped 10% of his height, or was too slow, then it would feel sluggish. Or they could just map their controls badly.

Unresponsive, floaty controls that you have to actively struggle with are my pet peeve, Rockstar and the Eurphoria Engine being a prime example. In GTA4 and RDR on foot controls feels like your character is a brick which you move by tugging on a string attached to it, very imprecise and at times extremely frustrating. I still love the shit out of RDR though, one of my favorite games ever.

Acceleration of absolute outputs (mouse).

Then there's delay from input to reaction, in both directions: some games have a delay between pressing a button and the result, some games have a delay between releasing a button and the result. The latter is much more common and noticeable in games such as The Witcher 3 or GTA 5 where the character does not stop moving instantly when you release the input. Usually this is implemented as a way to get realistic animation transitions from running to standing, but it feels clumsy because in real life you have pretty good control over your own muscles, and you know in advance where and when you want to stop running/walking. In games, the meaning of releasing the up key has always been "I want to stop here". The game cannot read your mind and decide to slow down a little bit before that, so either it makes stopping instantaneous, either you get a clunky character.

There's also unrebindable keys, modded keys/double taps/toggles/holds/mode switches/flight axes that you cannot configure, context-sensitive keys that should not be context sensitive and the reverse of that.

In fact you can even add bad UI. Action games that force you to pause all the time such as Skyrim with its threadbare favorite system. In fact, everything about the vanilla Skyrim UI is bad.

How well I'm able to control the camera used to be a big one for me, but nowadays it's more rare to find a game with shitty camera controls. Also, a shitty button layout without being able to customize it exactly how I want it. Sometimes games have multiple button layouts but they all don't feel just right
For bad controls for are having chunky movement, over sensitive aiming, and delayed in controller actions.

Well, if they outright don't work at all (or stop working at random because of random glitches), that's a reason. For example, the gyro controls in Mario & Luigi Dream Team often just failed outright; you'd be stuck in the same place on screen til the segment ended or you died horribly.

For controls that actually work mechanically... well, it's genre based. For an action game, tank controls (only going forward and back and turning the character round by holding left or right) simply aren't natural. For a racing game, it's when the cars slide across the screen all over the place (no friction at all). For a platform game or a fast paced game in general, then controls with any form of delay are a bad thing, like when an animation means your character only does something a whole second after the button is pressed.
